title: Functions — typing drills
description: Type function headers, a clamp, and an await. Spacing and indentation are flexible, and a trailing semicolon is fine.

drills.prompt: Declare a function named toggle_flashlight that returns nothing. Type only the header line.
drills.hint: Start with func, add empty parentheses, and you can mark the return type as -> void.
drills.explain: -> void means the function does not give a value back. It just does work, like flipping the flashlight.

drills.prompt: Declare a function named raise_fear that takes a float parameter named amount and returns nothing. Type only the header line.
drills.hint: Put the parameter in parentheses as amount: float, then optionally -> void and a colon.
drills.explain: The name amount is the input. A typed header helps Godot catch a call that passes the wrong kind of value.

drills.prompt: Write a line that sets fear to fear plus amount, clamped between 0.0 and max_fear.
drills.hint: Use clampf, which keeps a decimal number inside a range.
drills.explain: clampf stops fear from going below 0.0 or above max_fear. The similar clamp() function is also accepted here.

drills.prompt: Write an await that waits 0.5 seconds using a scene-tree timer.
drills.hint: await, then get_tree().create_timer(0.5).timeout — that is the usual Godot 4 pattern.
drills.explain: await pauses only the function that uses it. The rest of the game keeps running during the half-second wait.

drills.prompt: Write a function named get_fear that returns the fear variable as a float. Include the return line.
drills.hint: Two lines: a func header with -> float, then return fear. Tab is fine for the indent.
drills.explain: -> float tells callers they will get a decimal back. The body is just return fear.
